\begin{CRchronicle}{27}
Reed came on at Low Kiln without a boundary drawn: the yard turning. Work was a direction, never a figure, a bundle judged by the arm that carried it. A woman who asked what the reeds would cost was sent to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} Sella Vail instructed bucket, broom, pot and fire, never the basket, and said \emph{the house} where another woman would have said \emph{I}. The yard went around the unswept lines, the rack space and the place in the strip where a hand went in and did not come out: a look, a wide step and no number. The boy read it as a chart closed over an unopened note --- exact, complete, worth nothing.

Before first grey men came up the Clay Yard and went low-voiced into the back room; Jorra Vail gave them no name. He came through with grey slate dust ground into both forearms past the bent little finger, told a pot \emph{You’ll do} and withheld its note. His bent finger went into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, and the household straightened around his silence. The boy read the iron as holding and taking. Tarn took the broom only after it had been instructed; his seventh year stood held, and his stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check. Neither man named the other’s silence.

At the market the soft-cuffed clerk sat at the out-of-line landing with his slate to his forearm for a measure nobody called, and the trade went on over him. A foundling in cast-offs stood with silt pale in his wrists and a green sliver on a string at his throat. When a kiln-hand set a pot down his head went toward it half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and note, then stopped; he rubbed the sliver twice and let nothing out that a clerk could take down. No loaf passed and no slate was seen. The boy filed the delay as a thing that comes after the knock and is not a hearing.

On the third day bundles came in armfuls, and at the Weir a reed-cutter carried his tally in a cord, telling a woman who could not read it that the Court could not either. Mira Silt worked the eels, answered a thin run with \emph{Ask the river}, and let her thumb rest on the cord at her waist; her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string. Each evening Sella set the boy on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right, left the thread frozen and unwiped, told the fire it was the thaw and said \emph{The house will keep it}. Three days stood in his private file --- one hundred and twenty, one hundred and twenty-one and one hundred and twenty-two --- exact and unspent, as the river ran beyond the gap and the fire missed its fifth breath.
\end{CRchronicle}
